claims.claim: The crt-1; sel-12 animals showed improved response to light touch with a 77.7% response compared to 48.4% response of sel-12 animals.
claims.source: Consistent with the absence of neurodegenerative morphology of the mechanosensory neurons, the crt-1; sel-12 animals also showed improved response to light touch with a 77.7% response compared to 48.4% response of sel-12 animals (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: Loss of SEL-12 function results in deregulated ER Ca2+ release which promotes neuronal mitochondrial disorganization, enhanced OXPHOS and high ROS production which leads to neurodegeneration in sel-12 mutants.
claims.source: This suggests that loss of SEL-12 function results in deregulated ER Ca2+ release which promotes neuronal mitochondrial disorganization, enhanced OXPHOS and high ROS production which leads to neurodegeneration in sel-12 mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective rescue experiments showing that reducing ER Ca2+ release suppresses neurodegeneration.

claims.claim: Ca2+ uptake into the mitochondrial matrix is mediated by the highly conserved mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter.
claims.source: Ca2+ uptake into the mitochondrial matrix is mediated by the highly conserved mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter (Baughman et al., 2011; Csordás et al., 2013; De Stefani et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Baughman et al., 2011; Csordás et al., 2013; De Stefani et al., 2011.

claims.claim: mcu-1 null animals have reduced mitochondrial Ca2+ levels compared to wild type animals.
claims.source: In order to determine the effect the absence of the mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter has on mitochondrial Ca2+ levels, we measured mitochondrial Ca2+ levels and found that mcu-1 null animals have reduced mitochondrial Ca2+ levels compared to wild type animals (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: mcu-1; sel-12(ty11) animals show a reduction of mitochondrial Ca2+ load.
claims.source: Also, akin to our analyses of the crt-1; sel-12 and unc-68; sel-12 double mutants, mcu-1; sel-12(ty11) animals, show a reduction of mitochondrial Ca2+ load (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: The mcu-1 mutation improved the organization of neuronal mitochondria in sel-12 mutants.
claims.source: Furthermore, as we previously observed in the body wall muscle (Sarasija and Norman, 2015), we found that the mcu-1 mutation improved the organization of neuronal mitochondria in sel-12 mutants (Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: mcu-1; sel-12(ty11) animals show normal ROS and OCR levels similar to what was observed in sel-12 mutants with reduced ER Ca2+ release.
claims.source: Consistent with the improvement in mitochondrial structure and Ca2+ load, mcu-1; sel-12(ty11) animals also show normal ROS and OCR levels similar to what was observed in sel-12 mutants with reduced ER Ca2+ release (Figure 7C–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ROS and OCR measurements shown in Figure 7C-E.

claims.claim: Phenotypes of structural neurodegeneration such as ectopic sprouting, wave-like processes, lesions and breaks are decreased in the mcu-1; sel-12(ty11) animals compared with sel-12(ty11) mutants.
claims.source: Along with these observations, phenotypes of structural neurodegeneration such as ectopic sprouting, wave-like processes, lesions and breaks are also decreased in the mcu-1; sel-12(ty11) animals compared with sel-12(ty11) mutants (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claims.claim: The mcu-1; sel-12(ty11) animals show 78.8% response to light touch compared to 48.4% response of sel-12(ty11) animals.
claims.source: Moreover, the mcu-1; sel-12(ty11) animals show 78.8% response to light touch compared to 48.4% response of sel-12(ty11) animals (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: Reducing mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake normalizes mitochondrial metabolic activity and suppresses the neurodegenerative phenotype observed in sel-12(ty11) animals.
claims.source: Taken together these data suggest that reducing mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake normalizes mitochondrial metabolic activity and suppresses the neurodegenerative phenotype observed in sel-12(ty11) animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective rescue experiments with mcu-1 mutations.

claims.claim: Treatment of FAD fibroblasts with Ru360 resulted in a decrease of both ATP and ROS levels in these cells.
claims.source: Consistent with the improvement in mitochondrial function observed in the mcu-1; sel-12(ty11) animals, treatment of FAD fibroblasts with Ru360 resulted in a decrease of both ATP and ROS levels in these cells (Figure 7H,I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 7H,I.

claims.claim: drp-1(RNAi) rescues the mitochondrial structure in the sel-12(ty11) animals.
claims.source: While drp-1(RNAi) rescues the mitochondrial structure in the sel-12(ty11) animals (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), it is unable to restore mitochondrial calcium levels, OCR, and neurodegeneration (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: drp-1(RNAi) is unable to restore mitochondrial calcium levels, OCR, and neurodegeneration in sel-12(ty11) animals.
claims.source: While drp-1(RNAi) rescues the mitochondrial structure in the sel-12(ty11) animals (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A), it is unable to restore mitochondrial calcium levels, OCR, and neurodegeneration (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B–F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-F.

claims.claim: Defects in mitochondrial morphology may be a symptom but not the cause of the neurodegeneration observed in sel-12 mutants.
claims.source: This data suggests that defects in mitochondrial morphology may be a symptom but not the cause of the neurodegeneration observed in sel-12 mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the inability of drp-1(RNAi) to rescue neurodegeneration despite rescuing mitochondrial morphology.

claims.claim: sel-12(ty11) animals grown in the presence of doxycycline showed inhibition of mitochondrial function as evidenced by the suppression of the high mitochondrial respiration rate observed in sel-12 mutants.
claims.source: sel-12(ty11) animals grown in the presence of doxycycline showed inhibition of mitochondrial function as evidenced by the suppression of the high mitochondrial respiration rate observed in sel-12 mutants (Figure 8A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by OCR measurements shown in Figure 8A,B.

claims.claim: Doxycycline treatment rescued the mechanosensory defects in sel-12(ty11) animals, both in touch response and axon morphology.
claims.source: Interestingly, doxycycline treatment also rescued the mechanosensory defects in sel-12(ty11) animals, both in touch response and axon morphology (Figure 8C–E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral and morphological analysis shown in Figure 8C-E.

claims.claim: Doxycycline treatment reduced ATP and ROS levels as well as OCR in FAD fibroblasts.
claims.source: Consistent with FAD cells showing high mitochondrial activity, doxycycline treatment reduced ATP and ROS levels as well as OCR in FAD fibroblasts (Figure 8F–I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 8F-I.

claims.claim: Exacerbated ER Ca2+ transfer to the mitochondria boosts mitochondrial activity causing neurodegeneration in the sel-12 mutants.
claims.source: These data taken together with our observations of increased mitochondrial Ca2+ levels in sel-12 mutants and the ability of reducing Ca2+ transfer from the ER to the mitochondrial in suppressing the neurodegeneration associated with sel-12 mutants indicates that exacerbated ER Ca2+ transfer to the mitochondria boosts mitochondrial activity causing neurodegeneration in the sel-12 mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental data showing the relationship between ER-mitochondrial Ca2+ transfer, mitochondrial activity, and neurodegeneration.

claims.claim: sel-12(ty11) animals have elevated mitochondrial ROS compared to wild type animals.
claims.source: First, to investigate whether there is an elevation in mitochondrial ROS in the mechanosensory neurons undergoing neurodegeneration, we used a mitochondrial matrix targeted roGFP, a reduction-oxidation sensitive green fluorescent protein (Cannon and Remington, 2008; Melentijevic et al., 2017) and discovered that sel-12(ty11) animals have elevated mitochondrial ROS compared to wild type animals (Figure 9A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by roGFP measurements shown in Figure 9A.

claims.claim: sel-12(ty11) animals treated with 500 µM MitoTEMPO showed significant reduction in oxidized neuronal mitochondrial roGFP fluorescence levels.
claims.source: Consistent with MitoTEMPO reducing mitochondrial ROS levels without altering mitochondrial Ca2+ levels, we found that sel-12(ty11) animals treated with 500 µM MitoTEMPO showed significant reduction in oxidized neuronal mitochondrial roGFP fluorescence levels (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A) while mitochondrial Ca2+ levels remained similar to control sel-12(ty11) animals (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by roGFP measurements shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial Ca2+ levels in MitoTEMPO treated sel-12(ty11) animals remained similar to control sel-12(ty11) animals.
claims.source: Consistent with MitoTEMPO reducing mitochondrial ROS levels without altering mitochondrial Ca2+ levels, we found that sel-12(ty11) animals treated with 500 µM MitoTEMPO showed significant reduction in oxidized neuronal mitochondrial roGFP fluorescence levels (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A) while mitochondrial Ca2+ levels remained similar to control sel-12(ty11) animals (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Ca2+ measurements shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: sel-12(ty11) animals raised on MitoTEMPO show a decrease in the number of ectopic neuronal sprouts from two sprouts/ALM in control sel-12(ty11) animals to one sprouts/ALM.
claims.source: sel-12(ty11) animals raised on MitoTEMPO show a decrease in the number of ectopic neuronal sprouts from two sprouts/ALM in control sel-12(ty11) animals to one sprouts/ALM (Figure 9B) while TPP treated animals showed no such improvement (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: TPP treated sel-12(ty11) animals showed no improvement in ectopic neuronal sprouts.
claims.source: sel-12(ty11) animals raised on MitoTEMPO show a decrease in the number of ectopic neuronal sprouts from two sprouts/ALM in control sel-12(ty11) animals to one sprouts/ALM (Figure 9B) while TPP treated animals showed no such improvement (Figure 9B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claims.claim: MitoTEMPO treatment resulted in a normal behavioral response to light touch at 83.1% similar to wild type animals at 82.6% and much improved compared to the control and TPP treated sel-12(ty11) animals.
claims.source: Also, MitoTEMPO treatment resulted in a normal behavioral response to light touch at 83.1% similar to wild type animals at 82.6% and much improved compared to the control and TPP treated sel-12(ty11) animals (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral assay data shown in Figure 9C.

claims.claim: MitoTEMPO treatment does not rescue the mitochondrial morphology defects seen in sel-12(ty11) animals.
claims.source: However, MitoTEMPO treatment does not rescue the mitochondrial morphology defects seen in sel-12(ty11) animals (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that oxidative stress is not directly causing mitochondrial structural disorganization.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Oxidative stress is not directly causing mitochondrial structural disorganization.
claims.source: However, MitoTEMPO treatment does not rescue the mitochondrial morphology defects seen in sel-12(ty11) animals (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that oxidative stress is not directly causing mitochondrial structural disorganization.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the inability of MitoTEMPO to rescue mitochondrial morphology despite reducing ROS.

claims.claim: Deregulated Ca2+ transfer from the ER to the mitochondria increases OXPHOS resulting in superoxide generation triggering oxidative stress mediated neurodegeneration.
claims.source: Together our data suggest that deregulated Ca2+ transfer from the ER to the mitochondria increases OXPHOS resulting in superoxide generation triggering oxidative stress mediated neurodegeneration.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Mutations in sel-12 result in ER to mitochondria Ca2+ signaling defects, elevated mitochondrial Ca2+ levels, mitochondrial structural disorganization, dysfunction of mitochondrial metabolism and subsequent oxidative stress mediated neurodegeneration.
claims.source: In this study, we provide evidence that mutations in the gene encoding a C. elegans PSEN homolog, sel-12 result in ER to mitochondria Ca2+ signaling defects, elevated mitochondrial Ca2+ levels, mitochondrial structural disorganization, dysfunction of mitochondrial metabolism and subsequent oxidative stress mediated neurodegeneration.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the collective experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: The structural and functional neurodegeneration observed in sel-12 mutants are independent of the gamma-secretase activity of SEL-12.
claims.source: We also demonstrate that the structural and functional neurodegeneration observed in sel-12 mutants are independent of the gamma-secretase activity of SEL-12 and are a result of mitochondria generated superoxide that arise due to increased ER to mitochondria Ca2+ signaling resulting in amplified OXPHOS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experiments with gamma-secretase dead SEL-12 shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The neurodegeneration in sel-12 mutants is a result of mitochondria generated superoxide that arise due to increased ER to mitochondria Ca2+ signaling resulting in amplified OXPHOS.
claims.source: We also demonstrate that the structural and functional neurodegeneration observed in sel-12 mutants are independent of the gamma-secretase activity of SEL-12 and are a result of mitochondria generated superoxide that arise due to increased ER to mitochondria Ca2+ signaling resulting in amplified OXPHOS.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the collective experimental data showing the pathway from ER-mitochondrial Ca2+ transfer to ROS generation and neurodegeneration.

claims.claim: Skin fibroblasts isolated from FAD patients with mutations in PSEN1 show a similar mitochondrial phenotype as observed in C. elegans sel-12 mutants, demonstrating a conserved role of PSEN in mitochondrial regulation.
claims.source: Moreover, we show that skin fibroblasts isolated from FAD patients with mutations in PSEN1 show a similar mitochondrial phenotype as observed in C. elegans sel-12 mutants, demonstrating a conserved role of PSEN in mitochondrial regulation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the FAD fibroblast experiments shown in Figure 1E-H.

claims.claim: Increased mitochondrial Ca2+ aids in the allosteric activation of several TCA cycle enzymes, including pyruvate dehydrogenase α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and isocitrate dehydrogenase.
claims.source: Indeed, increased mitochondrial Ca2+ aids in the allosteric activation of several TCA cycle enzymes, including pyruvate dehydrogenase α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and isocitrate dehydrogenase (McCormack and Denton, 1993), stimulates the ATP synthase (complex V) (Das and Harris, 1990), α-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase (McCormack and Denton, 1993; Wernette et al., 1981) and the adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT) (McCormack and Denton, 1993; Mildaziene et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McCormack and Denton, 1993.

claims.claim: Increased mitochondrial Ca2+ stimulates the ATP synthase (complex V).
claims.source: Indeed, increased mitochondrial Ca2+ aids in the allosteric activation of several TCA cycle enzymes, including pyruvate dehydrogenase α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and isocitrate dehydrogenase (McCormack and Denton, 1993), stimulates the ATP synthase (complex V) (Das and Harris, 1990), α-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase (McCormack and Denton, 1993; Wernette et al., 1981) and the adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT) (McCormack and Denton, 1993; Mildaziene et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Das and Harris, 1990.

claims.claim: Increased mitochondrial Ca2+ stimulates α-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase.
claims.source: Indeed, increased mitochondrial Ca2+ aids in the allosteric activation of several TCA cycle enzymes, including pyruvate dehydrogenase α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and isocitrate dehydrogenase (McCormack and Denton, 1993), stimulates the ATP synthase (complex V) (Das and Harris, 1990), α-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase (McCormack and Denton, 1993; Wernette et al., 1981) and the adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT) (McCormack and Denton, 1993; Mildaziene et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McCormack and Denton, 1993; Wernette et al., 1981.

claims.claim: Increased mitochondrial Ca2+ stimulates the adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT).
claims.source: Indeed, increased mitochondrial Ca2+ aids in the allosteric activation of several TCA cycle enzymes, including pyruvate dehydrogenase α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and isocitrate dehydrogenase (McCormack and Denton, 1993), stimulates the ATP synthase (complex V) (Das and Harris, 1990), α-glycerophosphate dehydrogenase (McCormack and Denton, 1993; Wernette et al., 1981) and the adenine nucleotide translocase (ANT) (McCormack and Denton, 1993; Mildaziene et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McCormack and Denton, 1993; Mildaziene et al., 1995.

claims.claim: The increase in mitochondrial Ca2+ concentration results in the coordinated upregulation of the TCA cycle and OXPHOS machinery, allowing for increased oxygen consumption, and ATP and ROS production.
claims.source: Thus, the increase in mitochondrial Ca2+ concentration results in the coordinated upregulation of the TCA cycle and OXPHOS machinery, allowing for increased oxygen consumption, and ATP and ROS production.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge and the citations provided in the preceding sentences.

claims.claim: Mutations in sel-12 lead to deregulated ER and mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling resulting in increased mitochondrial Ca2+ levels, which promotes mitochondrial metabolic activity.
claims.source: Here, we discover that mutations in sel-12 lead to deregulated ER and mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling resulting in increased mitochondrial Ca2+ levels, which promotes mitochondrial metabolic activity.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Elevated metabolic activity elevates ROS levels in sel-12 mutants and the deleterious effects of ROS results in the emergence of structural and functional phenotypes of neurodegeneration.
claims.source: Additionally, we provide evidence that this elevated metabolic activity elevates ROS levels in sel-12 mutants and the deleterious effects of ROS results in the emergence of structural and functional phenotypes of neurodegeneration.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the ROS measurements and neurodegeneration phenotypes shown throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Upon reducing ER Ca2+ release or mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake, the mitochondria of sel-12 mutants are no longer disorganized and show normal OCR, and the high levels of ROS and neurodegenerative phenotypes observed in sel-12 mutants are suppressed.
claims.source: Upon reducing ER Ca2+ release or mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake, the mitochondria of sel-12 mutants are no longer disorganized and show normal OCR, and the high levels of ROS and neurodegenerative phenotypes observed in sel-12 mutants are suppressed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the rescue experiments shown in Figures 6 and 7.

claims.claim: SEL-12 activity is required for normal ER to mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling, proper mitochondrial function and mitochondrial superoxide maintenance.
claims.source: These data indicate that SEL-12 activity is required for normal ER to mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling, proper mitochondrial function and mitochondrial superoxide maintenance.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental data showing the effects of sel-12 mutations.

claims.claim: Several studies in a variety of PSEN FAD models as well as tissue samples isolated from AD patients have shown that loss of PSEN function leads to perturbed ER Ca2+ signaling.
claims.source: Consistent with PSENs having a role in ER Ca2+ regulation, several studies in a variety of PSEN FAD models as well as tissue samples isolated from AD patients have shown that loss of PSEN function leads to perturbed ER Ca2+ signaling (Chan et al., 2000; Green et al., 2008; Ito et al., 1994; Leissring et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2005; Tu et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies: Chan et al., 2000; Green et al., 2008; Ito et al., 1994; Leissring et al., 1999; Smith et al., 2005; Tu et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The mitochondria-associated ER membrane is a highly active subcompartment of the ER that is physically connected to the mitochondria and is critical for several metabolic functions, such as Ca2+ homeostasis, cholesterol metabolism and the synthesis and transfer of phospholipids between the ER and mitochondria.
claims.source: The mitochondria-associated ER membrane is a highly active subcompartment of the ER that is physically connected to the mitochondria and is critical for several metabolic functions, such as Ca2+ homeostasis, cholesterol metabolism and the synthesis and transfer of phospholipids between the ER and mitochondria.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about mitochondria-associated ER membrane.

claims.claim: Elevated ER to mitochondrial contact and crosstalk has been observed in PSEN1 and PSEN2 knockout cells, in cells expressing FAD mutant PSEN2, and in skin fibroblasts from FAD and sporadic AD patients.
claims.source: Importantly, elevated ER to mitochondrial contact and crosstalk has been observed in PSEN1 and PSEN2 knockout cells, in cells expressing FAD mutant PSEN2, and in skin fibroblasts from FAD and sporadic AD patients (Area-Gomez et al., 2012; Filadi et al., 2016; Kipanyula et al., 2012; Zampese et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Area-Gomez et al., 2012; Filadi et al., 2016; Kipanyula et al., 2012; Zampese et al., 2011.

claims.claim: There is an up regulation of OXPHOS, ATP production and ROS generation in skin fibroblasts isolated from FAD patients that can be reduced by inhibiting mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake.
claims.source: Although the functional importance of these observations has not been resolved, our analyses of skin fibroblasts isolated from FAD patients, indicates that there is an up regulation of OXPHOS, ATP production and ROS generation that can be reduced by inhibiting mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake, similar to what we observe in sel-12 mutants.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the FAD fibroblast experiments shown in Figure 1 and Figure 7H,I.

claims.claim: In sel-12 mutants neurodegeneration is caused by elevated ER to mitochondrial transfer of Ca2+.
claims.source: We also demonstrate that in sel-12 mutants neurodegeneration is caused by elevated ER to mitochondrial transfer of Ca2+.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the rescue experiments showing that reducing ER-mitochondrial Ca2+ transfer suppresses neurodegeneration.

claims.claim: PSEN function on the ER membrane is required for normal ER Ca2+ transfer to the mitochondria and in the absence of optimal PSEN function, excessive Ca2+ is transferred to the mitochondria leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and an elevation of mitochondrial generated superoxide radicals that promote neurodegeneration.
claims.source: Taken together, these data present an inclusive model that indicates that PSEN function on the ER membrane is required for normal ER Ca2+ transfer to the mitochondria and in the absence of optimal PSEN function, excessive Ca2+ is transferred to the mitochondria leading to mitochondrial dysfunction and an elevation of mitochondrial generated superoxide radicals that promote neurodegeneration (Figure 9D).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the collective experimental data and presented as a model in Figure 9D.

claims.claim: Recent analyses of PSEN1/2 knockout mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) have shown reduced mitochondrial activity suggesting PSEN function is vital for mitochondrial function.
claims.source: However, recent analyses of PSEN1/2 knockout mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), unlike our studies, have shown reduced mitochondrial activity suggesting PSEN function is vital for mitochondrial function (Contino et al., 2017; Pera et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Contino et al., 2017; Pera et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The reduction of mitochondrial function in PSEN1/2 KO MEFs could be rescued by PSEN2 and not PSEN1, implicating a role of PSEN2 in mitochondrial function in MEFs.
claims.source: Significantly, one of these studies demonstrated that the reduction of mitochondrial function in PSEN1/2 KO MEFs could be rescued by PSEN2 and not PSEN1, implicating a role of PSEN2 in mitochondrial function in MEFs (Contino et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Contino et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Astrocytes derived from iPSCs isolated from skin cells from patients with PSEN1 mutations showed elevated OCR and ROS production, which could be rescued by CRISPR/Cas9 repair of the PSEN1 mutation.
claims.source: While the reduced mitochondrial activity might appear to be at odds with our study, a recent analysis of astrocytes derived from iPSCs isolated from skin cells from patients with PSEN1 mutations also showed elevated OCR and ROS production, which could be rescued by CRISPR/Cas9 repair of the PSEN1 mutation (Oksanen et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Oksanen et al., 2017.

claims.claim: In day eight vs. day one adult sel-12 mutants a drastic reduction of mitochondrial activity was observed in comparison to aged matched wild type animals indicating that in aged animals mitochondria function becomes impaired in sel-12 mutants.
claims.source: Also of note, we did observe in day eight vs. day one adult sel-12 mutants a drastic reduction of mitochondrial activity in comparison to aged matched wild type animals indicating that in aged animals mitochondria function becomes impaired in sel-12 mutants, consistent with the decreased mitochondrial function as a result of PSEN mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by OCR measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: The impairment of mitochondrial function with age in sel-12(ty11) animals could be a result of increased mitochondrial activity resulting in ROS-mediated oxidative damage at earlier stages of adulthood.
claims.source: The impairment of mitochondrial function with age in sel-12(ty11) animals could be a result of increased mitochondrial activity resulting in ROS-mediated oxidative damage at earlier stages of adulthood.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the cause of age-related mitochondrial decline.

claims.claim: Gamma-secretase mediated cleavage is required for the activation of Notch signaling and emphasizes the critical role of PSEN in mediating Notch function.
claims.source: Gamma-secretase mediated cleavage is required for the activation of Notch signaling and emphasizes the critical role of PSEN in mediating Notch function (De Strooper et al., 1997).

claims.claim: It is the gamma-secretase mediated cleavage of APP that leads to the generation of Abeta peptides of various lengths, including the toxic Abeta42.
claims.source: Also, it is the gamma-secretase mediated cleavage of APP that leads to the generation of Abeta peptides of various lengths, including the toxic Abeta42 (Bezprozvanny and Mattson, 2008; Hardy, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bezprozvanny and Mattson, 2008; Hardy, 2006.

claims.claim: The role of SEL-12 in the regulation of mitochondrial function and nervous system fitness does not require gamma-secretase activity or Notch signaling.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Le Couteur et al., 2016.

claims.claim: C. elegans encodes a single APP-like protein, apl-1.
claims.source: Besides the usual strengths (e.g. rapid growth cycle, genetic manipulation, cell biological approaches, simple nervous system), C. elegans encodes a single APP-like protein, apl-1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about C. elegans genetics.

claims.claim: APL-1, like its APL-1 mammalian homologs (APLP1 and ALPL2), lack the Abeta peptide sequence.
claims.source: Unlike APP, APL-1, like its APL-1 mammalian homologs (APLP1 and ALPL2), lack the Abeta peptide sequence.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about APL-1 protein structure.

claims.claim: APL-1 lacks the beta-secretase recognition sequences and the C. elegans genome does not encode a beta-secretase.
claims.source: Furthermore, APL-1 lacks the beta-secretase recognition sequences and the C. elegans genome does not encode a beta-secretase; therefore, it is unlikely that C. elegans produce Abeta peptides (Daigle and Li, 1993; McColl et al., 2012) and indeed, no Abeta peptides have been detected in C. elegans (McColl et al., 2012).

claims.source: Furthermore, APL-1 lacks the beta-secretase recognition sequences and the C. elegans genome does not encode a beta-secretase; therefore, it is unlikely that C. elegans produce Abeta peptides (Daigle and Li, 1993; McColl et al., 2012) and indeed, no Abeta peptides have been detected in C. elegans (McColl et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McColl et al., 2012.

claims.claim: In the absence of Abeta, mutations in PSEN result in deregulated ER to mitochondria Ca2+ signaling that causes elevated mitochondrial Ca2+ which hyperactivates mitochondrial respiration leading to the accumulation of superoxides and the subsequent reduction of neuronal cell function and health.
claims.source: Excitingly, utilizing this experimental system, we find that in the absence of Abeta, mutations in PSEN result in deregulated ER to mitochondria Ca2+ signaling that causes elevated mitochondrial Ca2+ which hyperactivates mitochondrial respiration leading to the accumulation of superoxides and the subsequent reduction of neuronal cell function and health.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the collective experimental data from C. elegans studies.

claims.claim: Overexpression of human Abeta1-42 results in chemosensory defects, locomotor defects and touch defects in C. elegans.
claims.source: Overexpression of human Abeta1-42 results in chemosensory defects, locomotor defects (Ahmad and Ebert, 2017; Dosanjh et al., 2010; Fong et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2006) and touch defects (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies and data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Overexpression of human Abeta1-42 in the nervous system or body wall muscle results in the reduction of OXPHOS.
claims.source: Moreover, similar to the drastic reduction of OXPHOS we observe in older adult sel-12 mutants compared to age matched wild type animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D), recent studies have shown that overexpression of human Abeta1-42 in the nervous system or body wall muscle results in the reduction of OXPHOS (Fong et al., 2016; Sorrentino et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fong et al., 2016; Sorrentino et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The mechanism of Abeta1-42 overexpression appears distinct from presenilin mutations.
claims.source: However, there are some important distinctions between overexpression of human Abeta1-42 and mutations in sel-12. Although overexpression of human Abeta1-42 in the nervous system disrupts touch response similar to sel-12 mutants (Figure 5A), it fails to result in hallmark sel-12 mutation defects such as axonal morphology phenotypes, disorganized mitochondria, and excessive calcium loading (Figure 5B–E). Therefore, the mechanism of Abeta1-42 overexpression appears distinct from presenilin mutations.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of Abeta1-42 overexpression and sel-12 mutation phenotypes.

claims.claim: An initial insult in FAD is elevated ROS production from the mitochondria due to an increase in ER Ca2+ transfer.
claims.source: These important findings suggest that an initial insult in FAD, since C. elegans does not produce Abeta peptides, is elevated ROS production from the mitochondria due to an increase in ER Ca2+ transfer.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the C. elegans studies showing neurodegeneration without Abeta.

claims.claim: Abeta accumulation may be a secondary, albeit critical, component to the pathogenesis of the disease.
claims.source: Thus, Abeta accumulation may be a secondary, albeit critical, component to the pathogenesis of the disease.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the findings from C. elegans studies.

results.result: sel-12 mutants exhibit elevated mitochondrial Ca2+ levels in both body wall muscle and mechanosensory neurons. GCaMP6/mCherry fluorescence ratios are 2.4-fold and 3.4-fold higher in sel-12(ar131) and sel-12(ty11) mutants respectively compared to wild type in muscle, with similar elevations observed in ALM and PLM neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 provide consistent quantitative measurements of mitochondrial Ca2+ using ratiometric GCaMP6/mCherry imaging across multiple sel-12 alleles and tissue types (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B). The use of mCherry as an expression control strengthens the interpretation that differences reflect Ca2+ levels rather than expression variation. Multiple independent alleles showing similar phenotypes supports genetic specificity.

results.result: sel-12 mutants display elevated mitochondrial respiration with basal OCR of 5.5-6.4 pmol/min/worm compared to 3.9 pmol/min/worm in wild type, and maximal OCR of 10-11.7 pmol/min/worm compared to 7.2 pmol/min/worm in wild type. This indicates elevated OXPHOS activity resulting in higher OCR and ATP levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C38 present consistent OCR measurements across three independent sel-12 alleles using Seahorse XFp analysis (Figure 1C,D). The elevated basal and FCCP-stimulated maximal respiration rates are statistically significant and reproducible across alleles. The interpretation linking elevated OCR to OXPHOS activity is well-supported by the experimental design and is consistent with ATP measurements in C1B.

results.result: The elevated ATP, mitochondrial Ca2+, and OCR in sel-12 mutants are not due to increased mitochondrial biogenesis or accumulation, as mitoDNA copy number and TOM20::GFP fluorescence are similar between wild type and sel-12 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 address a critical alternative explanation through qRT-PCR of mitoDNA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) and TOM20::GFP fluorescence quantification (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F). Both measurements show no significant differences, supporting the conclusion that metabolic changes reflect altered mitochondrial function rather than mitochondrial number. This control strengthens the interpretation of the primary findings.

results.result: FAD patient fibroblasts with PSEN1 mutations show elevated ATP levels, increased basal and maximal OCR, and elevated ROS compared to control fibroblasts, demonstrating a conserved role of PSEN1 in mitochondrial activity similar to SEL-12 in C. elegans.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 demonstrate conservation of the mitochondrial phenotype in human cells (Figure 1E-H). The use of multiple FAD and control cell lines strengthens the findings. However, the manuscript does not specify sample sizes, number of biological replicates, or provide detailed information about the specific PSEN1 mutations in each line, which limits full evaluation. The parallel phenotypes across species support evolutionary conservation of PSEN function.

results.result: sel-12 mutants exhibit mitochondrial disorganization in mechanosensory neurons, with 53-55% showing discontinuous mitochondrial morphology compared to 16.7% in wild type, indicating that SEL-12 function is required to maintain mitochondrial structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 quantify mitochondrial morphology defects using mCherry-labeled mitochondria in mechanosensory neurons (Figure 2A). The significant increase in discontinuous morphology across two sel-12 alleles supports the conclusion. The claim is consistent with prior work cited (Sarasija and Norman, 2015) showing similar defects in other tissues, strengthening the interpretation of a general role for SEL-12 in mitochondrial structure.

results.result: sel-12 mutants show age-dependent mechanosensory defects, with normal responses at L4 larval stage but significantly reduced light touch responses (39-45% vs 83% in wild type) at day 1 of adulthood that progressively worsen by day 3.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 document a clear temporal progression of mechanosensory dysfunction using a well-established behavioral assay (Figure 2B). The normal L4 responses followed by adult-onset defects across three independent alleles strongly support a neurodegenerative rather than developmental defect. Statistical significance is indicated and sample sizes appear adequate (n values provided).

results.result: Pan-neuronal but not muscle-specific expression of wild type SEL-12 rescues mechanosensory defects in sel-12(ty11) mutants, demonstrating tissue-specific requirement for SEL-12 in neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58 provide tissue-specific rescue experiments (Figure 2C) that establish neuronal autonomy of the mechanosensory phenotype. The differential rescue by pan-neuronal versus muscle-specific promoters is a strong genetic control demonstrating where SEL-12 function is required. This is consistent with similar tissue-specific rescue of sprouting phenotypes (C64-C65).

results.result: sel-12 mutants exhibit age-dependent ectopic neuronal sprouting from ALM soma, with normal morphology at L4 but ~2 sprouts/soma at day 1 of adulthood increasing to ~3 sprouts/soma by day 3, compared to 0.56-1 sprouts/soma in age-matched wild type. These structural aberrations appear in adulthood rather than during development, indicating neurodegeneration rather than developmental defects.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C63, C69-C70 document progressive structural neurodegeneration using GFP-labeled neurons (Figure 3A,B). The temporal pattern—normal at L4 followed by adult-onset and progressive worsening—strongly supports a neurodegenerative interpretation. Quantification shows clear dose-response with age. The parallel between structural and functional decline (mechanosensation) strengthens the overall conclusion.

results.result: sel-12(ty11) mutants at day 1 of adulthood show multiple axonal abnormalities including wavy processes (~7 vs ~2 per 10 processes in wild type), lesions (~6 vs ~1 per 10), and breaks (~2 vs ~0 per 10).
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 quantify distinct morphological abnormalities in axonal processes (Figure 3A,C-E). The multiple independent structural defects all showing significant increases in sel-12 mutants provide convergent evidence for neurodegeneration. The quantification appears rigorous with adequate sample sizes indicated.

results.result: Notch receptor mutants (lin-12 and glp-1) show normal mechanosensation (78-86% response) at days 1-3 of adulthood similar to wild type (83%), indicating that Notch signaling is not required for mechanosensation.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 use genetic analysis of Notch pathway mutants to test whether mechanosensory defects require Notch signaling (Figure 4A). The normal touch responses in lin-12 and glp-1 mutants across multiple time points provide strong evidence that the sel-12 mechanosensory phenotype is Notch-independent. This is an important control given PSEN's known role in Notch processing.

results.result: Gamma-secretase inhibition with Compound E does not impair mechanosensation or cause neuronal sprouting, and a catalytically-dead SEL-12 (D226A) rescues both mechanosensory defects and neurodegenerative morphology comparably to wild type SEL-12, demonstrating that gamma-secretase activity is not required for mechanosensory neuronal integrity or function.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 use both pharmacological (Compound E) and genetic (D226A mutant) approaches to test gamma-secretase dependence (Figure 4B-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The convergent results from two independent methods strongly support the conclusion. The D226A rescue is particularly compelling as it demonstrates loss of catalytic activity (confirmed by egg-laying defect) while retaining rescue function. This is a critical finding distinguishing PSEN's role in neurodegeneration from its canonical gamma-secretase function.

results.result: Pan-neuronal Abeta1-42 overexpression causes mechanosensory deficits similar to sel-12 mutants but does not produce neuronal structural aberrations, mitochondrial disorganization, or elevated mitochondrial Ca2+, indicating a distinct mechanism from presenilin mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 compare Abeta overexpression to sel-12 phenotypes (Figure 5A-E). The selective overlap (touch defects) versus divergence (no structural/mitochondrial defects) provides important mechanistic insight. However, the interpretation that Abeta acts through a "distinct mechanism" is somewhat limited—Abeta overexpression is artificial and may not reflect endogenous Abeta function. The key conclusion that sel-12 neurodegeneration can occur without Abeta-like effects is well-supported.

results.result: Reducing ER Ca2+ release through crt-1 or unc-68 null mutations normalizes mitochondrial Ca2+ levels, improves mitochondrial organization, reduces OCR to wild type levels, and decreases ROS in sel-12 mutants, demonstrating that exacerbated ER Ca2+ release drives elevated OXPHOS and mitochondrial dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C92 present comprehensive rescue experiments targeting ER Ca2+ release (Figure 6A-F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The normalization of multiple downstream phenotypes (mitochondrial Ca2+, morphology, OCR, ROS) by two independent genetic manipulations (crt-1, unc-68) provides strong evidence for the proposed pathway. The logical progression from Ca2+ to metabolism to ROS is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Reducing ER Ca2+ release in crt-1;sel-12 and unc-68;sel-12 double mutants strongly suppresses neurodegeneration (ectopic sprouting, waves, lesions, breaks) and improves mechanosensation (77.7% vs 48.4% in sel-12 alone), indicating that deregulated ER Ca2+ release promotes neurodegeneration through mitochondrial dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C95 demonstrate functional rescue of neurodegeneration by reducing ER Ca2+ release (Figure 6G-H, supplementary figures). The suppression of multiple independent neurodegenerative phenotypes and restoration of mechanosensory function provide strong support for the causal pathway from ER Ca2+ dysregulation to neurodegeneration. This connects the upstream Ca2+ defects to the downstream neurological phenotypes.

results.result: Reducing mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake through mcu-1 null mutation normalizes mitochondrial Ca2+ levels, improves mitochondrial organization, reduces ROS and OCR, suppresses neurodegeneration (sprouting, waves, lesions, breaks), and restores mechanosensation (78.8% vs 48.4%) in sel-12 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C103 demonstrate rescue by blocking mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake (Figure 7A-G, Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The comprehensive rescue of metabolic, structural, and functional phenotypes by targeting a different node in the pathway (mitochondrial uptake vs ER release) strongly supports the proposed Ca2+-driven mechanism. The parallel results with crt-1/unc-68 experiments provide convergent evidence.

results.result: Treatment of FAD fibroblasts with Ru360 (mitochondrial Ca2+ uniporter inhibitor) decreases both ATP and ROS levels.
results.evaluation: Claim C104 demonstrates that the mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake mechanism is conserved in human FAD cells (Figure 7H,I). The pharmacological rescue in human cells parallels the genetic rescue in worms, supporting evolutionary conservation. However, limited methodological details are provided about the human cell experiments (replicates, controls, statistical tests).

results.result: drp-1 RNAi rescues mitochondrial morphology but fails to restore mitochondrial Ca2+ levels, OCR, or neurodegeneration in sel-12 mutants, suggesting that mitochondrial morphology defects are a symptom rather than cause of neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 use drp-1 knockdown to test whether mitochondrial morphology defects are causal (Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The selective rescue of morphology without functional improvement provides important mechanistic insight distinguishing correlation from causation. This negative result strengthens the overall model by ruling out an alternative explanation.

results.result: Doxycycline treatment inhibits mitochondrial function (suppresses elevated OCR) and rescues mechanosensory defects in sel-12 mutants. In FAD fibroblasts, doxycycline reduces ATP, ROS, and OCR, indicating that elevated mitochondrial activity drives neurodegeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C111 use pharmacological inhibition of mitochondrial function to test causality (Figure 8A-I). The rescue of neurodegeneration by directly reducing mitochondrial activity provides strong support for the model that excessive OXPHOS drives pathology. The parallel effects in worms and human cells strengthen the conclusion. However, doxycycline has pleiotropic effects beyond mitochondrial inhibition, which could complicate interpretation.

results.result: sel-12 mutants have elevated mitochondrial ROS in mechanosensory neurons. MitoTEMPO treatment reduces mitochondrial ROS without altering Ca2+ levels, decreases ectopic sprouting (from 2 to 1 sprout/ALM), and restores normal mechanosensation (83% vs 48% in untreated), while control TPP treatment shows no improvement.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 use mitochondria-targeted antioxidant to test whether ROS mediates neurodegeneration (Figure 9A-C, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A-B). The selective reduction of ROS without affecting Ca2+ levels, combined with functional rescue and appropriate TPP control, provides strong evidence that mitochondrial ROS is the proximal cause of neurodegeneration. This completes the mechanistic pathway from Ca2+ to OXPHOS to ROS to neurodegeneration.

results.result: MitoTEMPO treatment does not rescue mitochondrial morphology defects in sel-12 mutants, suggesting that oxidative stress does not directly cause mitochondrial structural disorganization.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 show selective rescue effects of MitoTEMPO (Figure 9—figure supplement 1C). The failure to rescue morphology while rescuing function helps order the pathological events and indicates that morphology defects may be parallel to rather than downstream of ROS. This nuanced finding strengthens the overall mechanistic model.

results.result: Mutations in sel-12 result in elevated ER-mitochondrial Ca2+ signaling leading to increased mitochondrial Ca2+ content, which stimulates mitochondrial respiration and increases superoxide production, ultimately causing oxidative stress-mediated neurodegeneration through a pathway involving ER to mitochondria Ca2+ transfer, amplified OXPHOS, and mitochondrial superoxide generation.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C120-C121, C123 synthesize the overall mechanistic model supported by the collective experimental evidence. The pathway is well-supported by: (1) direct measurements of elevated mitochondrial Ca2+, (2) elevated OXPHOS/OCR, (3) elevated ROS, (4) neurodegeneration phenotypes, and (5) rescue experiments targeting each step (ER Ca2+ release, mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake, ROS scavenging, OXPHOS inhibition). The logical progression and multiple lines of convergent evidence strongly support this integrative conclusion.

results.result: Neurodegeneration in sel-12 mutants occurs through faulty ER-to-mitochondria Ca2+ transfer and mitochondrial metabolic dysfunction, completely independent of Abeta signaling and gamma-secretase activity, as demonstrated in C. elegans which lack Abeta peptides.
results.evaluation: Claims C26, C122, C147, C154 establish Abeta-independence through multiple lines of evidence: (1) C. elegans lacks Abeta-encoding genes, (2) gamma-secretase inhibition doesn't phenocopy sel-12, (3) catalytically-dead SEL-12 rescues, (4) Abeta overexpression produces different phenotypes. This is a critical conceptual advance challenging the amyloid hypothesis. The evidence is strong, though the relevance to human AD where Abeta is present requires careful interpretation.

results.result: Aged sel-12 mutants (day 8 adults) show dramatically reduced mitochondrial respiration compared to wild type, indicating that mitochondrial function becomes impaired with age in sel-12 mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C39 and C143 document age-related decline in mitochondrial function (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D). This observation is interesting but somewhat tangential to the main findings. The interpretation that early hyperactivity leads to later decline is reasonable but speculative (C144). The data support the observation but mechanistic understanding is limited.

results.result: Skin fibroblasts from FAD patients with PSEN1 mutations show upregulation of OXPHOS, ATP production, and ROS generation that can be reduced by inhibiting mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake, demonstrating a conserved role of PSEN in mitochondrial regulation across species.
results.evaluation: Claims C124 and C137 establish evolutionary conservation of the mechanism (Figure 1E-H, Figure 7H-I). The parallel phenotypes in human FAD cells and rescue by Ru360 support conservation. However, the human cell work is less extensively characterized than the C. elegans studies. More details on cell line validation, mutation specifics, and experimental replication would strengthen confidence.
